displayQuote: I'd rather have roses on my table than diamonds on my neck

meta.title: Who really said "I'd rather have roses on my table than diamonds on my neck"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Emma Goldman everywhere — but the line is in none of her books, and no printed trace turns up before the 1970s. Here's what she actually wrote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'd rather have roses on my table than diamonds on my neck'?
meta.ogDescription: The roses-and-diamonds line appears in no Emma Goldman book or speech, and no source has ever been cited. What she really wrote — and where the fake came from.

answer.label: Not traced to Emma Goldman
answer.authorDates: Popularly credited to Emma Goldman, 1869–1940 · anarchist writer and orator
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears in none of Goldman’s published books — a full-text search of Living My Life (1931) and of Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) returns neither half of it — and Wikiquote does not list it for her in any section. Every printed appearance we could find is a modern quotation anthology or gift book that credits her with no source at all.

source.heading: No source, in any of her books

docMeta.dd: None — no book, speech, letter, diary or interview is named by any site that carries the line

source.excerpt: I did not believe that a Cause which stood for a beautiful ideal, for anarchism, for release and freedom from conventions and prejudice, should demand the denial of life and joy. I insisted that our Cause could not expect me to become a nun and that the movement should not be turned into a cloister. If it meant that, I did not want it. “I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody’s right to beautiful, radiant things.”
trail: The line is missing from Goldman’s own books. A full-text search of her 1931 autobiography Living My Life ↗ returns no “roses on my table” and no “diamonds on my neck”; the word “diamonds” occurs exactly once, in an unrelated memory of her father trying to marry her off.
Nor is it in her first book. Project Gutenberg’s text of Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) ↗ contains neither phrase.

The specialists have not adopted it either. Wikiquote’s Emma Goldman page ↗ does not carry the line in any section — not sourced, not disputed, not misattributed — and Quote Investigator ↗ has never published an article on it.

What the aggregators offer instead is nothing at all. Goodreads ↗ prints the line under Goldman’s name with no source and a notice that its quotes are community-added and unverified; AZQuotes ↗ gives no book, page, publisher or date.
source.excerptNote: This is not the roses-and-diamonds line — there is no source text for that one to quote. It is the passage from Goldman’s autobiography that carries the sentiment people are reaching for, and it is the same passage a T-shirt printer once compressed into her other famous fake, the “if I can’t dance” slogan.

sourceLink.text: Living My Life (1931), full text at The Anarchist Library

source.rightsNote: Rights follow the source, and this line has no identifiable source — no work, no date, no publisher — so no public-domain status can be claimed for it. The Goldman passage shown above is a separate matter: Living My Life was published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1931 and is not treated here as public domain; it is reproduced as a short quotation for criticism and comment.

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.heading: The woman the line is pinned on
author.metaLine: 1869–1940 · Anarchist writer and orator, deported from the United States in 1919
author.bio: Emma Goldman wrote and lectured on anarchism, free speech, marriage and prisons, was jailed repeatedly, and was deported from the United States in 1919. Her books include Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) and the autobiography Living My Life (1931). She is quoted constantly and sourced rarely — which is exactly how lines she never wrote came to travel under her name.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. The line is absent from Emma Goldman, Living My Life (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1931) and from Emma Goldman, Anarchism and Other Essays (1910). The earliest printed appearances found are late-twentieth-century quotation anthologies — e.g. Ashton Applewhite, Tripp Evans and Andrew Frothingham, And I Quote (1992), 83, which credits Goldman and gives no source.

misattribution.heading: The Goldman quote problem
misattribution.intro: Emma Goldman is one of the most quoted women on the internet and one of the most misquoted. The roses-and-diamonds line fits a pattern her scholars have documented for decades: a sentiment that sounds like her, tightened into a slogan by somebody else, printed on a shirt or a poster, and then repeated until it looks sourced.

items.why: No book, essay, speech, letter or interview has ever been named for it. It is absent from the full text of Living My Life ↗ and from Anarchism and Other Essays ↗, and Wikiquote ↗ does not carry it at all. Goodreads ↗ and AZQuotes ↗ both print it with no citation whatsoever.

“If I can’t dance I don’t want to be in your revolution” was not written by Goldman either. Her biographer Alix Kates Shulman described in Lilith ↗ how, in early 1973, the anarchist printer Jack Frager compressed the dancing episode from Living My Life into that slogan for a batch of T-shirts — and how it spread from there.
“If voting changed anything, it would be made illegal” is credited to her constantly. Wikiquote’s Disputed section ↗ records that there is no evidence she ever said it.

misattribution.truthLine: What Goldman actually wrote, in Living My Life ↗, was “I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody’s right to beautiful, radiant things” — the real sentence behind the sentiment, and nothing like the roses-and-diamonds wording.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: Goldman is an odd magnet for a line about table flowers. She wrote and spoke about marriage, prisons, free speech and political violence, was jailed repeatedly, and was deported from the United States in 1919. The sentiment — that beauty and joy are not luxuries to be postponed until after the revolution — is genuinely hers, and she put it in print. The sentence is not.

That gap is how quote fakes are made. Real prose is long, argumentative and hard to fit on a mug; a slogan written in the author’s voice travels better. With Goldman this happened once in the open, and someone wrote down exactly how: her biographer watched an anarchist printer boil a page of the autobiography down to a single line for a T-shirt run, and the line went on to be reprinted everywhere as Goldman’s own.
context.detailsSummary: The paper trail, such as it is
detailsBody: Searching Google Books for the phrase turns up nothing published in Goldman’s lifetime. The oldest match the index returns is Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations (1977), which Google matches but does not let you read. The oldest readable snippets are 1990s compilations: a 1992 quotation collection, a 1995 gift book of women’s sayings, and a 1998 book about baths and beauty products — each printing the line under Goldman’s name with nothing behind it.

The wording is also unstable, which is the usual sign that no original exists to anchor it. The 1992 anthology has “diamonds around my neck”; the 1995 one has “I would rather have roses…”; other printings drop the “my” and put the roses “on the table.” A sentence that a writer actually wrote tends to come down in one shape.
context.pull: The sentiment is hers. The sentence is not.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Emma Goldman page contains neither "roses on my table" nor "diamonds on my neck" in any section; it carries the sourced Living My Life line "I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody's right to beautiful, radiant things"; and its Disputed section states there is no evidence Goldman said "If voting changed anything, it would be made illegal."

The complete text of Living My Life (Knopf, 1931) contains neither "roses on my table" nor "diamonds on my neck" — the sole occurrence of "diamond" is "her in silks and diamonds" in an unrelated passage about her father — and it does contain the dancing episode ending "I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody's right to beautiful, radiant things."
The Anarchist Library hosts the full text of Emma Goldman's Living My Life, sourced to New York: Alfred A. Knopf Inc., 1931.
Project Gutenberg's full text of Anarchism and Other Essays contains neither "roses on my table" nor "diamonds on my neck".
Project Gutenberg's catalogue record identifies Anarchism and Other Essays as Emma Goldman's first published book, 1910.

Alix Kates Shulman recounts that in early 1973 the anarchist printer Jack Frager condensed the dancing episode of Living My Life into the T-shirt slogan "If I can't dance I don't want to be in your revolution," which Goldman never wrote; the article was published in Lilith and a different version appeared in Women's Review of Books, December 1991.

Goodreads prints "I'd rather have roses on my table than diamonds on my neck" under Emma Goldman's name with no book or source cited, plus a notice that quotes are added by the community and not verified.
AZQuotes prints the quote under Emma Goldman's name with no source, book, page, publisher or year displayed.
A site search of Quote Investigator returns no article about "I'd rather have roses on my table than diamonds on my neck".

Google Books returns no appearance of the phrase before Laurence J. Peter's Peter's Quotations (1977, p. 507, no preview available); the earliest readable snippets are And I Quote (Applewhite/Evans/Frothingham, 1992, p. 83, wording "diamonds around my neck"), Brilliance: Uncommon Voices from Uncommon Women (1995, p. 32, "I would rather have roses..."), and Victoria Bath & Beauty (Leslie George, 1998, p. 65) — all crediting Emma Goldman with no source.
